sections.title: In brief
sections.text: Past and present editors reflect on the journal and the design-science field ten years after the inaugural editorial. Knight is one of the credited authors.

sections.title: Retrospective question
sections.text: What has the journal and its community accomplished, and what challenges should design research address next?

sections.title: Knight’s position
sections.text: Knight again interprets design science as studying design. She defends the field’s own history and diverse methods, including systematic analysis and improvisational practice, while emphasizing social, intellectual, bodily and perceptual human capacities.

sections.title: How the contribution was assembled
sections.text: Editors were invited to reflect independently, with constraints on length and references. The authors explicitly declined to harmonize or synthesize the statements, unlike the 2015 editorial.

sections.title: Knight’s examples
sections.text: She points to an expanded range of design-related disciplines at MIT and describes teaching generative work through shape and making grammars using hand, eye and touch.

sections.title: Her concluding direction
sections.text: Knight argues that studying these human forms of designing can contribute to broader efforts in design research. Her remarks about automation are a reflective position and teaching observation, not a benchmark comparing people with AI.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: There is no single experimental method or consensus conclusion across this editorial. Claims from one contributor should not be attributed to every author. The opening retrospective does not substitute for a systematic evaluation of the field.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Compare Knight’s 2015 and 2025 statements: the commitment to broad, rigorous design study continues, with renewed attention to what human generative activity involves.
